question: Can an auxiliary language model synthesize short executable programs that reproduce pretrained Transformer attention matrices, and do alignment and head-replacement results establish explanation plausibility, predictive validity, causal localization, or adversarial faithfulness?

key_findings.claim: The pipeline produces an unusually large, inexpensive library of executable attention proxies, but the search space and final explanations inherit strong priors from one synthesis model and a sparse summary of each target head.
key_findings.evidence: For every head, the method sends Claude Sonnet 4 an approximately 4,000-token prompt containing only the top 2.5% attention weights on TinyStories examples, validates an initial Python program using NumPy, spaCy, or NLTK, and performs one best-versus-worst-example refinement using Jensen-Shannon distance. Fewer than 4,000 candidates, about 35 million input and 3.5 million output tokens, and roughly $150 yield 1,664 final programs: 144 each for BERT-Base and GPT-2 Small, 704 for TinyLlama-1.1B, and 672 for Llama-3.2-3B. This is practical coverage, not exhaustive symbolic identification.

anchors.section: 2.2 Generating Functional Proxies via Program Synthesis

key_findings.claim: The synthesis and evaluation objectives differ, but global library reranking may select and report on the same unspecified held-out IoU set, creating a winner's-curse risk rather than a clearly independent test.
key_findings.evidence: Initial/refined candidates are selected with Jensen-Shannon distance, Equation 2, while attention alignment uses weighted Intersection over Union, Equation 3. The paper says pi-star is chosen on D_val and separately calls the TinyStories IoU subset held out, but gives no split diagram, counts, sampling scheme, or confirmation that global best-program search over 144-704 programs is scored on a fresh test set. If the same held-out examples select and evaluate the global winner, the large library mechanically inflates fit and its size confounds the apparent model-scale trend. No alternate synthesis-run uncertainty is reported.

key_findings.claim: Many synthesized programs visibly reproduce coarse attention structure, yet individual examples also hallucinate structure; therefore attention-map fit supports proxy plausibility without validating a program's docstring or semantic interpretation.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 2 juxtaposes real matrices, program matrices, and program excerpts for GPT-2, TinyLlama, and BERT. Several capture diagonal, previous-token, first-token, or linguistic patterns, while the caption explicitly notes hallucinated structure such as a diagonal in the BERT proxy. A readable conditional in code can be inspected and falsified, but no independent human audit checks whether the code's apparent rule is complete, whether its natural-language label is correct, or whether the program behaves as intended outside sampled matrices.

key_findings.claim: Selecting the best program from the entire model-wide library often improves over each head's intended synthesized program, revealing both reusable symbolic motifs and a head-identification failure mode.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 3 compares the program generated for a head with the globally highest-IoU program among all programs for that model. The global-best median is visibly higher in all four models, with approximate medians near 34 versus 25 for BERT, 67 versus 51 for GPT-2, 74 versus 40 for TinyLlama, and 79 versus 55 for Llama-3.2; the paper reports mean global-best IoU of 69%, 74%, and 79% for the decoder models. A generic first-token, local, or diagonal program can therefore outperform a head-conditioned explanation, which weakens any claim that synthesis recovered that head's unique algorithm.

key_findings.claim: The discussion's 'up to 99% mean IoU' wording is not a model-wide average and should not be conflated with the reported aggregate fit.
key_findings.evidence: Section 3.1 reports mean best-program IoU of 69% for GPT-2, 74% for TinyLlama, and 79% for Llama-3.2, while Figure 3 shows individual best-program distributions extending toward 99-100%. Page 9 then says model-level analyses achieve up to 99% mean IoU without identifying a model, head subset, or aggregation that has that mean. The visible evidence supports some near-perfect head/program fits and substantially lower model means, not a 99% mean characterization of a model.

key_findings.claim: Higher alignment in the larger decoder models is not an identified model-scale effect because architecture, training, head count, causal masking, and candidate-library size all vary together.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 3 orders BERT-Base, GPT-2 Small, TinyLlama-1.1B, and Llama-3.2-3B and observes higher global-best IoU for the three causal decoders as nominal size rises. BERT is an encoder with bidirectional masks, while the others differ in architecture, tokenizer, data, training recipe, and number of heads; the global candidate pool also grows from 144 programs to 704 or 672. With one checkpoint per family and no controlled width/depth scaling series, the plot cannot isolate scale as the cause of simpler or more specialized attention.

key_findings.claim: The category analysis offers a plausible depth narrative for GPT-2 attention, but the categories are themselves synthesized from program docstrings and clustered by the same kind of language-model judgment rather than independently validated behavior.
key_findings.evidence: The authors cluster synthesized-program docstrings into categories and show that early GPT-2 layers contain more first-token patterns while deeper layers contain more syntactic patterns. Figure 4 separately sorts rows within the similarity and category panels, so visual cells cannot be traced one-to-one across the two halves. Because a language model generated both code and semantic summaries and no blind annotators or counterfactual category tests are reported, this establishes explanation plausibility, not ground-truth functional taxonomy.

key_findings.claim: Program replacement is a real causal intervention on the attention matrix and shows sufficiency for some behavior, but it does not localize a head's complete causal function or show that the selected program is the unique faithful explanation.
key_findings.evidence: At inference the method replaces A=softmax(QK-transpose/sqrt(dk)) with pi(X), ranks heads by IoU, and greedily replaces the best-fitting fraction. Figure 5's legend reports Spearman correlations of -0.915 for GPT-2 and -0.999 for TinyLlama and Llama-3.2 between IoU and substitution cost. However, only attention weights are replaced: value vectors, OV transformations, residual paths, downstream compensation, and redundant heads remain learned. Preserving loss therefore shows that the proxy supplies enough routing in context, not that code captures the complete head computation, necessity, semantics, or unique mechanism.

key_findings.claim: The lower-diagonal replacement control demonstrates that naive symbolic patterns can fail catastrophically, but it is too narrow to rule out generic program priors or redundancy as explanations of successful replacement.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 5 compares learned program replacements with a uniform lower-triangular or lower-diagonal causal-attention baseline; the baseline's perplexity can exceed a 1,000% increase after replacing only about 5% of heads in TinyLlama, while fitted programs degrade more slowly. This is a useful negative control against one fixed matrix, but the global-best analysis already shows generic programs transfer across heads. Random same-IoU matrices, matched local/first-token baselines, program mutations, and swapping equally aligned programs across functional categories are not tested.

key_findings.claim: Downstream multiple-choice results suggest substantial behavioral tolerance to symbolic replacement, but do not support a uniform claim across all models, tasks, or replacement fractions.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 6 evaluates HellaSwag, PIQA, SciQ, ARC-Easy, SocialIQA, and COPA while replacing heads in descending IoU order. Its legend and plotted series cover GPT-2, TinyLlama, and Llama-3.2 despite prose referring to all four models, and curves vary materially by task; occasional gains at low replacement are consistent with pruning noisy heads. The abstract reports up to 25% replacement for a 16% perplexity increase and the discussion says several QA tasks preserve performance around 30-40%, but there are no confidence intervals, repeated synthesis seeds, significance tests, matched pruning controls, or BERT downstream curves.

key_findings.claim: Attention-level predictive validity on unseen corpora and constructions remains untested even though cumulative program substitutions receive a useful downstream OOD behavioral test.
key_findings.evidence: TinyStories is chosen for simple, structured text and is used to extract patterns, synthesize programs, measure held-out attention IoU, and measure perplexity during replacement. Figure 6 then carries the frozen proxy ranking into six QA datasets and tests aggregate task accuracy, which is genuine behavioral distribution shift. However, attention alignment and individual program-head substitution cost are never remeasured there, so the study cannot tell whether the programs still predict the target heads' routing or which proxy will fail on news, code, dialogue, long context, multilingual text, or adversarial constructions.

key_findings.claim: The paper contains no adversarial faithfulness test: it neither searches for inputs where a program and head disagree nor tests whether a plausible-looking program can be spoofed while preserving selected metrics.
key_findings.evidence: The one refinement round uses naturally occurring best and worst TinyStories examples, and replacement follows ordinary held-out IoU ranking. There is no optimization over tokens, lengths, parses, or prompt formats to maximize proxy-head divergence; no counterexample-guided synthesis loop; no adversarially mutated program; and no evaluation of a target model strategically hiding or changing its computation. Consequently the study supports readable proxy plausibility and limited attention-level causal sufficiency, not adversarial robustness or explanation faithfulness in a deceptive setting.

key_findings.claim: The appendix heatmaps show that fit quality is heterogeneous rather than a general symbolic account of every attention head, with BERT particularly weak and several decoder heads still poorly approximated.
key_findings.evidence: Full per-head alignment heatmaps in the appendix show many dark low-IoU cells alongside high-alignment bands; BERT has the weakest overall coverage, while TinyLlama and Llama-3.2 still contain low-fit regions. The author limitations explicitly state that many programs fall below 40% similarity and that occasional replacement improvements likely reflect pruning. Thus the strongest conclusion concerns a substantial subset of routings, not complete model-level program extraction.

key_findings.claim: The released-paper configuration is not immutably reproducible and even the target Llama checkpoint is named inconsistently.
key_findings.evidence: The main text alternates 'Llama-3B' with 'Llama-3.2-3B'; only the appendix name plus 28-layer/24-head dimensions identifies the likely family. Claude Sonnet 4, BERT, GPT-2, TinyLlama, and Llama revisions are not pinned; neither are TinyStories examples/splits, seeds, spaCy/NLTK versions, prompt templates, downstream scoring protocol, or generated-program hashes. Page 10 gives a mutable GitHub repository URL but no commit or release. As a result, 1,664 assignments, library reranking, and six-task curves cannot be reconstructed exactly from the PDF pin alone.

anchors.section: 2.2 synthesis model, tools, and library totals

method.core_idea: Use an auxiliary language model to synthesize executable token-to-attention Python functions from sparse examples of each pretrained attention head, rerank programs by matrix alignment, and substitute high-alignment programs for neural attention matrices to test behavioral sufficiency.
method.mechanism: The target model supplies attention matrices on TinyStories. The top 2.5% of weights are serialized into prompts, Claude Sonnet 4 proposes code and receives one contrastive refinement round, candidates are selected by Jensen-Shannon distance, and held-out weighted IoU measures fit. For causal replacement, pi(X) replaces the learned softmax QK matrix while the head's value and output paths remain intact; heads are replaced greedily from highest IoU downward and model perplexity or multiple-choice accuracy is measured.
assumptions: An attention matrix is an appropriate explanatory boundary even though it omits value vectors, OV maps, residual interactions, and downstream nonlinear computation.
The top 2.5% of attention weights retain the behavior needed to infer a head's routing rule.
TinyStories supplies representative linguistic structures for synthesis, selection, perplexity testing, and transfer to the six downstream tasks.
Python with NumPy, spaCy, and NLTK is expressive enough for the target patterns while remaining meaningfully human-readable.
Claude Sonnet 4's code and linguistic priors do not create misleading generic motifs that look explanatory without being head-specific.
One initial candidate and one refinement round adequately search a large, non-identifiable program space.
The examples used to choose a global best program are independent from those used to report its IoU, although the split relation is not specified.
Held-out matrix IoU is a useful predictor of behavioral substitution quality despite not measuring values or complete head outputs.
Greedy replacement in descending IoU provides interpretable marginal evidence despite changing the context in which later heads are evaluated.
Behavior preservation under replacement indicates causal sufficiency, but does not by itself imply necessity, uniqueness, or semantic correctness.
Multiple-choice accuracy and TinyStories perplexity are sensitive enough to expose functionally important proxy errors.

techniques.role: Compresses the strongest token-pair weights into a textual synthesis prompt.
Generates executable Python proxies conditioned on observed attention examples.
Uses best- and worst-fitting examples to revise each initial program once.
Scores and chooses executable candidates using distributional divergence.
Evaluates held-out overlap between real and synthesized attention matrices.
Tests whether a program synthesized for any head can better explain another head.
Replaces the learned QK attention matrix while retaining learned value and output computation.
Accumulates interventions from highest to lower attention alignment.
Summarizes recurring symbolic motifs and their layer distribution.

evaluations.setting: All 1,664 head assignments in BERT-Base, GPT-2 Small, TinyLlama-1.1B, and Llama-3.2-3B, synthesized and evaluated on TinyStories (PDF pp. 3-6)
evaluations.metric: Held-out weighted IoU between real and program attention matrices.
evaluations.result: The globally best model-library program often exceeds the intended head-conditioned program; reported mean global-best IoU is about 69% for GPT-2, 74% for TinyLlama, and 79% for Llama-3.2, while BERT and a nontrivial tail of decoder heads remain weak.
evaluations.baseline: Random-token, random-column, uniform/lower-diagonal attention, and the intended program; split sizes and independence of global selection from final IoU reporting are not specified.

evaluations.setting: Selected GPT-2, TinyLlama, and BERT heads with real matrices, synthesized matrices, and code excerpts.
evaluations.metric: Qualitative structural agreement and visible proxy errors.
evaluations.result: Programs reproduce recognizable local, diagonal, first-token, and linguistic motifs, but also hallucinate features such as a BERT diagonal.
evaluations.baseline: Direct visual inspection of the target attention matrix.

evaluations.setting: GPT-2 program library grouped by language-model-generated docstrings across layers.
evaluations.metric: Category frequency and program-attention similarity heatmaps.
evaluations.result: Early layers appear richer in first-token rules and later layers in syntactic rules, but the panels are independently sorted and categories lack external validation.
evaluations.baseline: No human-coded or counterfactual behavioral category baseline.

evaluations.setting: Greedy attention-matrix replacement on TinyStories for GPT-2, TinyLlama, and Llama-3.2.
evaluations.metric: Percent perplexity increase versus fraction of heads replaced; Spearman association with IoU.
evaluations.result: Fitted programs degrade more gradually than the fixed causal lower-diagonal control; Figure 5 reports Spearman correlations of -0.915, -0.999, and -0.999 respectively. The introduction states that as many as 25% of heads can be replaced for only a 16% perplexity increase but does not tabulate the aggregation behind that summary.
evaluations.baseline: Uniform lower-diagonal attention replacement and the unmodified model.

evaluations.setting: Six multiple-choice datasets: HellaSwag, PIQA, SciQ, ARC-Easy, SocialIQA, and COPA, for three decoder models under increasing replacement.
evaluations.metric: Task accuracy relative to the unreplaced model.
evaluations.result: Several model-task curves preserve much of their accuracy through roughly 30-40% replacement, while others fall sooner and a few initially improve; no uncertainty, repeated synthesis seed, or matched pruning curve is shown.
evaluations.baseline: The original model at zero replacement; no random-head or attention-pruning baseline in Figure 6.

evaluations.setting: Per-head heatmaps for GPT-2 in the main text and BERT, TinyLlama, and Llama-3.2 in the appendix (PDF pp. 6, 13-15).
evaluations.result: High-fit structure is widespread but heterogeneous, with conspicuous low-alignment cells and much weaker coverage in BERT.
evaluations.baseline: Within-model comparison of intended and globally reranked program fit.

limitations: Author-stated: many synthesized programs remain below 40% attention similarity, so a large fraction of heads lack good symbolic proxies.
Author-stated: some low-fraction replacements improve behavior, plausibly because the intervention prunes noisy heads rather than faithfully explaining them.
Author-stated: richer search and multi-round refinement could improve the limited one-revision synthesis procedure.
Reviewer-identified: TinyStories is used throughout synthesis, alignment selection, and perplexity intervention, with no attention-level out-of-distribution test.
Reviewer-identified: dataset split sizes, example counts, sequence-length distribution, seeds, and synthesis-run variance are not reported.
Reviewer-identified: it is unclear whether global best-program selection and its reported IoU use independent data, so reranking over 144-704 candidates may create a winner's-curse bias.
Reviewer-identified: only the attention matrix is symbolized; value vectors, OV maps, residual-stream routing, MLPs, and cross-head interactions remain neural.
Reviewer-identified: global best-program gains reveal non-identifiability and generic motif reuse, so head-conditioned code is not necessarily the recovered algorithm.

Reviewer-identified: all causal replacement figures omit BERT despite page 8 claiming the downstream result holds across all four architectures, and include no confidence intervals, seeds, or statistical tests.
Reviewer-identified: the fixed lower-diagonal baseline is not matched to IoU, locality, sparsity, or program complexity and cannot isolate semantic faithfulness.
Reviewer-identified: model size is confounded with architecture, causal masking, training, tokenizer, head count, and candidate-pool size.
Reviewer-identified: the 99% 'mean IoU' discussion wording is inconsistent with the explicitly reported model means of 69%, 74%, and 79%.
Reviewer-identified: executable Python is testable but no formal specification or proof verifies the programs, despite the paper's formal-verifiability motivation.
Reviewer-identified: no adversarial counterexample generation, program mutation, strategic model, or explanation-spoofing evaluation tests faithfulness under pressure.
Reviewer-identified: the mutable GitHub URL has no commit/release pin, model/API snapshots and NLP dependencies are unspecified, and Llama-3B versus Llama-3.2-3B naming is inconsistent.
failure_modes: A generic first-token or local-attention program can score well for many heads and be mistaken for a head-specific explanation.
Top-2.5% filtering can omit diffuse but behaviorally important attention mass, making the synthesized code brittle even when salient edges align.
The synthesis model can hallucinate diagonal or linguistic rules and encode them in readable code, increasing plausibility without improving faithfulness.
Behavior can remain stable after an incorrect head replacement because other heads and residual paths compensate for the intervention.
Greedy cumulative replacement changes the residual state, so later replacement effects need not equal the head's effect in the original model.
Programs that fit short, simple TinyStories inputs can fail on long sequences, rare syntax, code, multilingual text, or domain-specific tokenization.
A high attention IoU can still alter low-mass edges that interact with high-value vectors, while a lower IoU proxy can preserve the head output by matching important value-weighted edges.
Task accuracy can hide systematic behavioral changes through coarse aggregation or chance on small multiple-choice datasets.
The program space admits many extensionally similar functions on observed examples but sharply different counterfactual behavior.
Global reranking can select a chance high-IoU program from a larger library and then report that same selection-set score as apparent generalization.
A changed Claude/API or spaCy/NLTK version can synthesize or execute different programs under the unpinned workflow.
reusable_insights: Executable explanations permit literal component substitution, which is stronger than evaluating natural-language labels alone when the intervention boundary is stated precisely.
Use one objective for synthesis and a different held-out metric for evaluation to reduce direct metric overfitting, while still reporting selection details and uncertainty.
Compare a target-conditioned explanation with the best explanation from a shared library; a large gap is a practical identifiability warning and a route to discovering reusable motifs.
Separate attention-routing sufficiency from complete-head causality: replace A, AV, and the full OV output in staged interventions to locate where a symbolic approximation remains faithful.
Alignment should be tested with adversarially generated counterexamples, matched generic priors, and program mutations before readable code is treated as a robust explanation.
Measure predictive validity prospectively by freezing programs and predicting which unseen corpora, tasks, or prompts will exhibit head-specific failures before running interventions.
Occasional gains under replacement should trigger explicit pruning controls rather than being folded into evidence for explanation quality.
Reserve a final untouched test set after global library reranking; otherwise candidate-pool size becomes an unmeasured source of optimistic fit.
open_questions: Do programs selected on TinyStories preserve attention alignment, perplexity, and task behavior on long-context, code, multilingual, and adversarially composed inputs?
How many distinct programs remain observationally equivalent on held-out examples but diverge on counterfactual token sequences?
Does value-weighted output alignment predict behavioral replacement better than attention IoU?
Would replacing the full head output, rather than only its attention matrix, preserve the apparent causal sufficiency?
Can counterexample-guided iterative synthesis discover failures that one natural best/worst refinement round misses?
Do independent human annotators agree that synthesized programs are understandable, and can their semantic labels predict unseen attention behavior?
Does the apparent scale trend persist in a controlled same-family checkpoint series with fixed data and candidate budget?
Can a strategically trained model route behavior through components that defeat this program-synthesis audit while preserving plausible proxies?
How do program complexity and minimum-description length trade off against held-out alignment and intervention fidelity?

competitive_landscape.title: Attention is not Explanation
competitive_landscape.relationship: Foundational attention-faithfulness challenge and direct non-identifiability comparator.
competitive_landscape.difference: Jain and Wallace show that attention can be uncorrelated with importance and that very different attention distributions can yield equivalent predictions. Hayes et al. improve on purely observational attention by substituting executable matrices, but behavior preservation still demonstrates one sufficient routing surrogate rather than a unique explanation of the complete computation.

competitive_landscape.title: Compositional Explanations of Neurons
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest same-coauthor predecessor using symbolic expressions to approximate component behavior.
competitive_landscape.difference: Mu and Andreas search compositional logical concepts for vision/NLI neurons, relate them to behavior, and use them to generate predictable adversarial examples. The reviewed work scales from neuron predicates to executable attention-matrix Python in modern LMs and performs substitution, but does not match the predecessor's adversarial predictive test or independently validate its semantic categories.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Transformer Programs
competitive_landscape.difference: Friedman et al. train a constrained Transformer that automatically decompiles into a discrete program, then use code-analysis tools on algorithmic and NLP tasks. Hayes et al. uniquely work post hoc on ordinary pretrained LMs, but only decompile attention routing while values, outputs, MLPs, and residual interactions remain neural; it therefore has broader checkpoint applicability and weaker end-to-end semantics.

competitive_landscape.title: Opening the AI black box: program synthesis via mechanistic interpretability
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest direct predecessor extracting executable Python from learned neural algorithms.
competitive_landscape.difference: Michaud et al.'s MIPS converts RNNs on 62 algorithmic tasks into finite-state machines and applies Boolean/integer symbolic regression, solving 32 tasks and extracting a more end-to-end algorithm. Hayes et al. use an LLM to scale proxy synthesis to 1,664 attention-head assignments in pretrained LMs, but their programs capture only the A matrix and are not validated for exact algorithm recovery.

competitive_landscape.title: Towards Understanding the Nature of Attention with Low-Rank Sparse Decomposition
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest prior attention-component replacement and decomposition competitor in modern LLMs.
competitive_landscape.difference: LoRSA learns a sparse replacement for multi-head attention, disentangles induction, successor, sink, and arithmetic components in models including Llama-3.1-8B, and evaluates interpretability/circuit discovery. Hayes et al. produce unrestricted human-readable Python without retraining the target, but approximate individual observed attention matrices and omit value-weighted or circuit-level decomposition. The two approaches compete directly on whether replacement structure yields interpretable attention components.

competitive_landscape.title: Can Interpretation Predict Behavior on Unseen Data?
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest current primary standard for prospective predictive validity under distribution shift.
competitive_landscape.difference: Li et al. use in-distribution attention patterns to predict which OOD rule hundreds of synthetic Transformers follow and explicitly decouple predictive value from causal support. Hayes et al. do behavioral replacement on six unseen task datasets, but never remeasure proxy-head alignment there or prospectively predict which inputs/programs will fail; its attention-level validation remains TinyStories-only.

competitive_landscape.title: Analyzing Multi-Head Self-Attention: Specialized Heads Do the Heavy Lifting, the Rest Can Be Pruned
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct head-importance, linguistic-specialization, and pruning baseline.
competitive_landscape.difference: Voita et al. show many heads can be removed with little performance loss—for example 38 of 48 encoder heads for only 0.15 BLEU—and that important heads often have interpretable roles. Hayes et al. replace rather than remove high-IoU heads, but without a matched pruning or random-head curve it cannot separate program fidelity from redundancy or beneficial pruning.

competitive_landscape.title: Validating Mechanistic Interpretations: An Axiomatic Approach
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest formal standard for deciding whether a mechanistic interpretation captures network semantics compositionally.
competitive_landscape.difference: Palumbo et al. formulate axioms inspired by abstract interpretation and validate interpretations on a known case and a Transformer 2-SAT solver. Hayes et al. provide executable substitution but test no completeness/compositionality axioms: a Python matrix proxy can preserve selected behavior while omitting values, OV maps, and compensating circuits. This primary comparator narrows the paper's 'formal description' rhetoric.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper introduces language-model-driven synthesis of executable explanations for every attention head in four pretrained Transformers and validates them by directly replacing neural attention with symbolic programs.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The distinctive combination is inexpensive LLM synthesis, 1,664 head assignments over four pretrained models, model-wide program reuse, held-out matrix alignment, and literal A-to-pi(X) interventions with perplexity and six-task curves. Earlier work already searches logical component explanations, decompiles constrained Transformers or algorithmic RNNs into Python, replaces/decomposes attention with sparse components, and establishes pruning and attention non-identifiability.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: High novelty for scaling unrestricted executable post-hoc proxies to ordinary pretrained-LM attention and connecting global library search to live matrix substitution. Moderate evidence that some attention-routing patterns are readable and behaviorally sufficient. Low evidence for complete or formally verified head functions: BERT has no intervention, only A is symbolized, reranking independence is unclear, aggregate means are 69-79% rather than 99%, semantic labels are unaudited, and no adversarial or attention-level OOD test exists. The defensible novelty is the synthesis-and-substitution workflow at scale, not program extraction in general or complete functional characterization of 30-40% of heads.

reviewer_notes: Independent second reviewer read all 15 pages of the exact arXiv:2606.19317v2 source, including Equations 1-3, every figure/heatmap, appendix, reference, limitation, and the mutable software link. The official v2 PDF (2026-06-29) is byte-identical to the cached source at SHA-256 cee300043efe488cabdf1ae13e76d46743fb183be0ccdd30cda0377491a01e19; v1 has different bytes and was not the reviewed source. The extraction is pinned by e8b38a8da1527fbe092c1057fc99f37a959864c7e5a5b9e55e6e7c6178aa8edc. This pass corrected a false appendix-example locator, removed an unsupported disjoint-split assumption, added the global-reranking winner's-curse audit, distinguished individual near-100% fits from 69/74/79% model means, documented the all-four-versus-three-decoder intervention contradiction, and added checkpoint/artifact reproducibility limits. Eight exact-version official primary competitors were rechecked through 2026-08-23.

Corrected split, locator, aggregate-IoU, model-coverage, and reproducibility mismatches rather than rubber-stamping them.
